title: Bacterial Meningitis: Isolate, Treat, Watch ICP
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Suspected bacterial meningitis is a neurologic and infectious emergency. Use indicated droplet precautions promptly, assess for sepsis and increased intracranial pressure, obtain ordered cultures without delaying life-saving antibiotics, and escalate neurologic decline immediately.
recognize: Fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting, altered mental status, or petechial/purpuric rash can occur.
Infants and older adults may have atypical presentations such as irritability, lethargy, poor feeding, or confusion.
Seizure, focal deficit, or declining consciousness suggests complicated disease.
priorities: Initiate transmission precautions according to suspected organism and facility policy.
Assess ABCs, hemodynamics, neurologic status, pupils, rash, and seizure activity.
Administer ordered antimicrobials rapidly and support sepsis management when present.
assessMonitor: Trend level of consciousness, vital signs, oxygenation, urine output, seizure activity, sodium, and signs of increased ICP or shock.
interventions: Reduce excess stimulation when severe headache or ICP concern is present.
Prepare for lumbar puncture only when clinically appropriate; urgent treatment should not wait for LP when delay would be unsafe.
medicationSafety: Antibiotic selection is age/risk specific and clinician directed.
Dexamethasone may be used in selected bacterial meningitis cases when timed appropriately with antibiotics.
teaching: Close contacts may need public-health-directed prophylaxis depending on the organism; follow current local guidance.
delegationScope: Isolation support may involve the whole team, but acute neurologic assessment and deterioration require licensed-nurse evaluation and immediate escalation.
examTrap: Delaying antibiotics until after every diagnostic test is completed in an unstable patient with suspected bacterial meningitis.
oneLinePearl: Meningitis: isolate, treat fast, and watch the brain and perfusion.

title: Guillain-Barré Syndrome: Weakness Can Reach the Airway
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Guillain-Barré syndrome can progress rapidly from ascending weakness and areflexia to respiratory failure and autonomic instability. Frequent respiratory and cardiac monitoring is more important than waiting for profound paralysis.
recognize: Symmetric weakness often begins in the legs and moves upward.
Paresthesias and reduced or absent reflexes are common.
Autonomic dysfunction may cause major blood-pressure swings, tachycardia, bradycardia, or dysrhythmias.
priorities: Assess respiratory effort, cough strength, ability to handle secretions, swallowing, and progression of weakness.
Use continuous cardiac/hemodynamic monitoring when disease is progressing or autonomic symptoms are present.
Escalate declining respiratory function before oxygen saturation becomes severely abnormal.
assessMonitor: Trend vital capacity/respiratory measures when ordered, bulbar symptoms, motor strength, autonomic signs, pain, and DVT risk.
interventions: Prepare for IVIG or plasma exchange as ordered.
Provide DVT prevention, pressure-injury prevention, eye/skin care, and communication support during weakness.
medicationSafety: Routine corticosteroids are not an effective primary treatment for classic GBS.
Sedatives and opioids require extra respiratory caution in a patient with neuromuscular weakness.
teaching: Recovery often takes time; rehabilitation and prevention of immobility complications are part of treatment.
delegationScope: Routine turning and skin care may be delegated, but respiratory or autonomic changes require immediate licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Assuming normal oxygen saturation means respiratory muscles are still strong.
oneLinePearl: In GBS, measure strength of breathing—not just oxygen saturation.

title: Myasthenia Gravis: Fatigable Weakness and Crisis
bottomLine: Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable skeletal-muscle weakness that improves with rest. New dysphagia, weak cough, inability to manage secretions, or respiratory weakness suggests myasthenic crisis and requires urgent airway-focused escalation.
recognize: Ptosis, diplopia, facial weakness, dysarthria, dysphagia, and limb weakness often worsen with activity.
Sensation is generally preserved.
Infection, surgery, medication changes, or missed therapy can precipitate crisis.
priorities: Assess respiratory effort, cough, secretions, swallowing, speech, and fatigue pattern.
Schedule demanding activities and meals around peak strength when possible.
Escalate bulbar or respiratory deterioration immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory measures when ordered, aspiration risk, nutrition, mobility, medication timing, and infection signs.
interventions: Administer pyridostigmine and immunotherapy as ordered.
Use aspiration precautions and texture modifications when prescribed.
medicationSafety: Excess cholinesterase inhibitor can cause muscarinic symptoms and weakness; medication changes require clinician direction.
Some antibiotics, magnesium, beta blockers, and other drugs can worsen neuromuscular transmission in susceptible patients; verify safety before administration when concerns arise.
teaching: Take medications on schedule and seek early care for infection or worsening swallowing/breathing.
delegationScope: Routine ADL assistance may be delegated when stable; swallowing or respiratory deterioration requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Giving a sedating medication to a patient with worsening bulbar weakness before reassessing ventilation.
oneLinePearl: MG gets weaker with use; crisis threatens swallow and breathing first.

title: Parkinson Disease: Mobility, Swallowing, Medication Timing
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Parkinson care depends on preserving mobility, swallowing, communication, bowel function, and exact medication timing. Abruptly delaying dopaminergic therapy can markedly worsen rigidity and function.
recognize: Bradykinesia, resting tremor, rigidity, shuffling gait, freezing, reduced facial expression, and soft speech are common.
Dysphagia and orthostatic hypotension create aspiration and fall risk.
Cognitive change, hallucinations, and sleep problems may occur.
priorities: Give time-critical medications at the prescribed schedule.
Assess swallowing, falls, orthostasis, constipation, and ability to perform ADLs.
Use mobility aids and cueing strategies rather than rushing the patient.
assessMonitor: Trend response to levodopa timing, dyskinesias, hallucinations, orthostasis, swallowing safety, nutrition, and bowel function.
interventions: Encourage regular mobility and therapy exercises.
Use aspiration precautions and speech/swallow therapy recommendations when indicated.
medicationSafety: Levodopa may cause dyskinesia, nausea, hallucinations, and orthostasis.
Do not abruptly stop dopaminergic therapy without clinician direction because severe rigidity and systemic deterioration can occur.
redFlags: Acute severe rigidity after medication interruption
teaching: Medication timing is part of mobility treatment; use fall prevention and allow extra time for movement.
delegationScope: Routine mobility assistance may be delegated after the plan is established; new swallowing or medication-response problems require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Giving levodopa hours late because the medication does not appear time-critical.
oneLinePearl: Parkinson medications are clock-sensitive—late doses can mean lost function.

title: Multiple Sclerosis: Relapse, Fatigue, and Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Multiple sclerosis can cause episodic or progressive neurologic dysfunction. Distinguish a true new relapse from temporary worsening caused by infection, heat, exhaustion, or other stressors, and prioritize mobility, bladder/bowel, vision, fatigue, and fall safety.
recognize: Common problems include visual changes, sensory symptoms, weakness, spasticity, imbalance, bladder dysfunction, and fatigue.
Heat and infection can temporarily worsen prior symptoms without new inflammatory disease.
New sustained focal neurologic symptoms require evaluation.
priorities: Assess whether symptoms are new, how long they have lasted, infection/fever, mobility, vision, swallowing, and bladder function.
Promote energy conservation and safe activity rather than prolonged immobility.
Escalate new severe neurologic deficits or infection.
assessMonitor: Trend strength, gait, falls, urinary retention/infection, skin integrity, vision changes, and medication adverse effects.
interventions: Use cooling strategies and rest periods when heat worsens symptoms.
Support PT/OT, bladder programs, and assistive devices as prescribed.
medicationSafety: Corticosteroids may shorten recovery from selected acute relapses but do not replace disease-modifying therapy.
Disease-modifying therapies can alter immune function and require drug-specific infection and laboratory monitoring.
teaching: Balance activity with fatigue management, avoid overheating when it worsens symptoms, and report sustained new neurologic deficits.
delegationScope: Routine ADL and mobility assistance may be delegated; new neurologic changes require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Assuming every temporary symptom flare during fever represents a new MS relapse.
oneLinePearl: MS symptoms can flare with heat or infection—look for the trigger before calling it a relapse.

title: Autonomic Dysreflexia: Sit Up and Remove the Trigger
bottomLine: Autonomic dysreflexia in a patient with a high spinal cord injury can cause severe hypertension, pounding headache, sweating/flushing above the injury, and bradycardia or tachycardia. Sit the patient upright, loosen constriction, find and relieve the trigger—often bladder or bowel—and escalate immediately.
recognize: A sudden BP rise above the patient's baseline is key.
Bladder distention or catheter obstruction is a common trigger; bowel impaction, skin pressure, tight clothing, and procedures can also trigger episodes.
Symptoms above and below the injury may differ because of disrupted autonomic pathways.
priorities: Sit upright with legs dependent when possible to lower BP.
Check urinary catheter tubing and bladder distention first, then other noxious triggers.
Monitor BP frequently and notify the emergency team/provider if hypertension persists.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, heart rate, headache, sweating/flushing, bladder output, bowel status, and skin pressure sources.
interventions: Remove restrictive garments and address the identified trigger using the established bowel/bladder plan.
Administer rapid-acting antihypertensive therapy if ordered when BP remains dangerously elevated.
medicationSafety: Avoid lying the patient flat during the hypertensive episode unless another emergency requires it.
Topical or rapid-acting antihypertensive choices depend on protocol and contraindications.
teaching: Patients and caregivers should know common triggers and carry an emergency plan when recommended.
delegationScope: Basic trigger checks may be assisted by trained staff, but autonomic dysreflexia requires immediate licensed-nurse assessment and escalation.
examTrap: Laying a severely hypertensive spinal-cord-injury patient flat and waiting for the provider before checking a kinked catheter.
oneLinePearl: AD: sit up, check bladder, remove trigger, recheck BP fast.
sourceBasis: Paralyzed Veterans of America Autonomic Dysreflexia Clinical Practice Guideline

title: Psychosis: Safety, Reality-Based Communication, Medication Effects
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: With psychosis, assess safety first—especially command hallucinations, paranoia, severe agitation, or inability to meet basic needs. Do not argue with delusions; acknowledge the patient's experience while maintaining a calm, reality-based stance.
recognize: Hallucinations are sensory experiences without an external stimulus; delusions are fixed false beliefs.
Negative symptoms can include flat affect, social withdrawal, low motivation, and reduced speech.
Substance use, delirium, mood disorders, neurologic illness, and medication effects can mimic primary psychosis.
priorities: Ask whether voices are giving commands and whether the patient intends to act on them.
Reduce stimulation and use simple, nonthreatening communication.
Maintain clear boundaries and escalate violence or self-harm risk.
assessMonitor: Trend sleep, intake, hydration, self-care, hallucination content, agitation, medication adherence, and extrapyramidal/metabolic adverse effects.
interventions: Use short concrete statements and avoid whispering or side conversations around a paranoid patient.
Support structured routine and participation in treatment when the patient can engage.
medicationSafety: Antipsychotics can cause EPS, tardive dyskinesia, orthostasis, metabolic effects, QT prolongation, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Clozapine requires specific blood-monitoring and infection precautions.
teaching: Medication adherence and follow-up reduce relapse risk; report fever, severe stiffness, involuntary movements, or major metabolic changes.
delegationScope: Observation may be assigned, but risk assessment and medication-effect evaluation require licensed-nurse judgment.
examTrap: Trying to prove to a paranoid patient that the delusion is impossible through prolonged debate.
oneLinePearl: Do not validate the delusion; validate the distress and keep communication grounded.

title: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome: Fever, Rigidity, Autonomic Instability
bottomLine: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a life-threatening reaction most often associated with dopamine-blocking drugs. High fever, severe generalized rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability, and elevated CK require stopping the offending drug and emergency supportive treatment.
recognize: NMS usually evolves over hours to days after starting, increasing, or changing dopamine-blocking therapy, but timing varies.
Rigidity is typically prominent and can be accompanied by tachycardia, labile BP, diaphoresis, and confusion.
Rhabdomyolysis can lead to acute kidney injury.
priorities: Hold the suspected causative medication and activate emergency medical evaluation.
Assess ABCs, temperature, rhythm, perfusion, rigidity, mental status, and urine output.
Begin cooling, IV fluids, and complication management as ordered.
assessMonitor: Trend temperature, CK, renal function, electrolytes, urine output, rhythm, and hemodynamics.
interventions: Prevent aspiration, pressure injury, and DVT during severe rigidity/immobility.
Prepare for ICU-level monitoring and drug-specific treatment when ordered.
medicationSafety: Do not simply administer the next antipsychotic dose because agitation or confusion persists.
Restarting antipsychotic therapy after NMS requires clinician-directed timing and selection.
teaching: Patients with prior NMS should tell future prescribers and seek urgent care for recurrent fever/rigidity after dopamine-blocking medication exposure.
delegationScope: NMS is an emergency requiring immediate licensed-nurse assessment and provider/rapid-response escalation.
examTrap: Treating high fever and rigidity as routine agitation from schizophrenia and giving another antipsychotic dose.
oneLinePearl: Antipsychotic + fever + lead-pipe rigidity = stop and escalate.

title: Serotonin Syndrome: Clonus, Agitation, Hyperthermia
bottomLine: Serotonin syndrome is caused by excess serotonergic activity and often presents rapidly with agitation, autonomic instability, hyperreflexia, tremor, and clonus. Stop serotonergic agents and escalate severe symptoms immediately.
recognize: Clonus and hyperreflexia strongly support serotonin toxicity, especially in the lower extremities.
Diaphoresis, diarrhea, fever, tachycardia, hypertension, and agitation are common.
Risk rises when multiple serotonergic drugs or interacting substances are combined.
priorities: Hold suspected serotonergic medications and assess ABCs, temperature, neurologic findings, rhythm, and hemodynamics.
Begin cooling, IV fluids, and benzodiazepine sedation when ordered for significant agitation.
Escalate hyperthermia, severe rigidity, seizure, or instability.
assessMonitor: Trend temperature, clonus/hyperreflexia, CK, renal function, electrolytes, rhythm, and urine output in severe cases.
interventions: Remove excess external heat and avoid physical restraint that can increase muscle activity when safer sedation is available.
Prepare for higher-level airway support in severe toxicity.
medicationSafety: SSRIs/SNRIs, MAOIs, tramadol, linezolid, dextromethorphan, some migraine drugs, and other serotonergic agents can interact.
Cyproheptadine may be used in selected cases under clinician direction.
teaching: Review prescription, OTC, and herbal products for serotonergic combinations and seek care for rapid agitation, tremor/clonus, fever, or diarrhea after medication changes.
delegationScope: Medication-toxicity assessment is a licensed-nurse responsibility; severe findings require immediate escalation.
examTrap: Confusing serotonin syndrome with NMS despite prominent clonus and hyperreflexia after serotonergic medication exposure.
oneLinePearl: Serotonin syndrome is fast and twitchy: clonus, hyperreflexia, autonomic heat.
sourceBasis: FDA product labeling for serotonergic agents

title: Major Depression: Function, Safety, and Treatment Response
bottomLine: Major depression is more than sadness; it affects sleep, appetite, concentration, energy, function, and sometimes safety. Always assess suicide risk directly, support basic self-care, and monitor for treatment response and activation after medication changes.
recognize: Depressed or irritable mood, loss of interest, sleep/appetite change, guilt, low energy, slowed or agitated behavior, impaired concentration, and suicidal thinking can occur.
Older adults may present with somatic complaints, functional decline, or cognitive symptoms.
Bipolar disorder should be considered when there is a history of mania or hypomania.
priorities: Assess suicide risk, psychosis, ability to eat/drink, sleep, substance use, and functional impairment.
Create a simple structured plan for hygiene, nutrition, activity, and rest.
Escalate inability to maintain safety or severe psychotic/catatonic features.
assessMonitor: Trend mood, sleep, appetite, energy, suicidal thinking, adherence, and medication adverse effects.
interventions: Use brief achievable goals rather than overwhelming demands.
Encourage psychotherapy and social support as part of the treatment plan.
medicationSafety: Antidepressants may take time for full effect; early activation or increased suicidal thinking requires prompt reassessment.
Antidepressant monotherapy can be problematic in bipolar disorder and requires diagnostic review.
teaching: Continue treatment as prescribed, keep follow-up appointments, and report worsening suicidal thinking or marked agitation after medication changes.
delegationScope: Routine supportive activities may be assigned, but suicide-risk and mental-status assessment require licensed-nurse judgment.
examTrap: Assuming a sudden increase in energy early in treatment means suicide risk has resolved.
oneLinePearl: Depression care tracks safety and function—not mood alone.
